read.sections.0.heading.source: Belonging is more than being there
read.sections.0.heading.back: Belonging is not only being present

read.sections.0.text.note: Ubuntu kept as a name and its saying translated as 'một người là người nhờ có những người khác'. Check the saying is rendered in the form Vietnamese readers meet it, and that 'miền nam châu Phi' is fine for 'southern Africa'. 'bị lờ đi hoặc bị gạt ra ngoài' for 'ignored or left out'.
read.sections.0.text.source: Belonging is the feeling of being accepted and connected to a group. A person can sit in a room with a group and still feel ignored or left out. People can belong to many kinds of groups at once, such as a class, a sports team, a group of friends or a club. It might also be people who share a language or a hobby. Many cultures value these connections. In southern Africa, people often talk about Ubuntu. It is usually explained as “a person is a person through other people”. It means we grow as people through our relationships with others.
read.sections.0.text.back: The feeling of belonging is the feeling of being accepted by a group and attached to that group. A person can sit in the room with the whole group and still feel ignored or pushed outside. Each person can belong to many groups at the same time, for example a classroom, a sports team, a group of friends or a club. It can also be people who speak the same language or share an interest. Many cultures value these bonds. In southern Africa, people often talk about Ubuntu. People often explain that "a person is a person because of other people". That means we grow thanks to our relationships with others.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Check it is simple enough and keeps the same ideas as the standard text.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: Belonging means you feel accepted in a group. You feel connected to the people in it. A person can be in a room and still feel left out. People can belong to many groups. It can be a class, a team or friends. It can be people who share a language or a hobby. In southern Africa, people talk about Ubuntu. It means we grow as people through other people.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: The feeling of belonging means you feel you are accepted by a group. You feel attached to the people in the group. A person can be in a room and still feel pushed outside. People can belong to many groups. It can be a class, a team or a group of friends. It can be people who speak the same language or share an interest. In southern Africa, people talk about Ubuntu. Ubuntu means we grow thanks to other people.

read.sections.1.text.note: 'thói quen sinh hoạt' for 'routines': in Vietnamese youth groups 'sinh hoạt' means the group's regular activities. Alternatives: nề nếp, thông lệ. 'nội quy' for 'rules' (a club's own rules).
read.sections.1.text.source: A barrier is something that makes it harder for someone to take part. Look at the youth club's feedback cards. One member finds meetings difficult when everyone speaks at once. Another member only joined after someone explained the rules quietly. The club does not need to change its members. Instead, it can change how it works. Turn-taking rules make meetings easier to follow, because only one person speaks at a time. A welcome partner can explain the club's routines to new members. These changes remove barriers, so more people can participate.
read.sections.1.text.back: A barrier is something that makes it harder for someone to take part. Look at the feedback cards of the youth club. One member finds it hard to keep up with the meeting when everyone talks at once. Another member only joined after someone gently explained the rules. The club does not need to change the members. Instead, the club can change its way of working. A take-turns rule makes the meeting easier to follow, because at any moment only one person speaks. A welcome buddy can explain the club's routines to new members. These changes remove barriers, so more people can take part.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: Glossary word 'thói quen sinh hoạt' kept in the simpler text as the checker requires; check it is understandable for slow readers.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: A barrier makes it hard to take part. Read the club's cards. One person finds it hard when everyone talks at once. One person joined after someone explained the rules. The club does not need to change its members. It can change how it works. With turn-taking, one person speaks at a time. A welcome partner can explain the routines. Now more people can join in.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A barrier makes it hard for someone to take part. Read the club's cards. One friend finds it hard when everyone talks at once. One friend only joined after someone explained the rules. The club does not need to change the members. The club can change its way of working. When people take turns, at any moment only one person speaks. A welcome buddy can explain the routines to a new friend. Thanks to that, more people can join in together.

read.sections.2.text.note: 'quyền chủ động' for 'agency' follows KEY_TERMS. 'Công ước của Liên Hợp Quốc về quyền trẻ em' for the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child: check the official Vietnamese name. 'ý kiến' for 'opinions'.
read.sections.2.text.source: Belonging also grows when people have a real say. One card says: “I want to help choose the activities, not only attend them”. A student planning group gives members more agency, which means the power to make choices and act. The UN agreement on children's rights says children have the right to give their opinions on things that affect them. It also says they can join or set up groups. A good group asks members what is working and what is not. Nobody should have to share private things about their life to belong.
read.sections.2.text.back: The feeling of belonging also grows when everyone has a real voice. One card says: "I want to choose the activities together, not just come to attend". A planning group of students gives members more agency, meaning the right to make choices and act on their own. The United Nations convention on the rights of the child says children have the right to speak their opinion about matters that affect them. The convention also says children can join or form groups. A good group asks its members what is going well and what is not going well yet. No one has to share private matters of their life in order to belong.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: Check that 'quyền chủ động' is understandable here with its explanation 'tự lựa chọn và hành động'.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Belonging grows when people have a say. One member wants to help choose what the club does. A planning group gives members more agency. They can make choices and act. A UN agreement says children have a right to give their opinions. They can join groups or start them. A good group asks what works and what does not. No one has to share private things to belong.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: The feeling of belonging grows when everyone has a voice. One member wants to choose together what the club does. A planning group gives members more agency. They can make choices and act on their own. A United Nations convention says children have the right to speak out their opinion. Children can join a group or set up a group. A good group asks what is going well and what is not going well yet. No one has to share private matters in order to belong.

watch.summary.note: Describes young people's own views on identity and belonging in school. 'bản sắc', 'quyền chủ động' and 'Những người đi trước' (for 'older helpers', i.e. mentors) need a native check. The last two sentences say learners do not have to share their own story; keep them exactly. | Review: 'Những người đi trước biết giúp đỡ' (older helpers) is slightly ambiguous; check it reads as older mentors.
watch.summary.source: In this video, young people talk about identity, belonging and agency in the places where they learn. Their identity grows from their experiences. These include goals they reached and mistakes they learned from. Belonging grows when adults know students' names. It also grows when students can share their work and not be judged. For them, agency means feeling sure that you can reach a goal if you work at it. Older helpers, friends and chances to lead can help. At the end, they tell adults that young people are ready to help shape their own lives and schools. The speakers share their own stories, but you do not need to share yours. You can think about the questions using the youth club, or a group you know.
watch.summary.back: In this video, young people talk about identity, belonging and agency in the places where they study. Each person's identity grows from their own experiences, including goals achieved and mistakes learned from. The feeling of belonging grows when adults know the students' names. It also grows when students can share their work without being judged. For them, agency means being convinced that you can reach your goals if you try hard. Helpful role models, friends and chances to be a leader can all help. At the end of the video, they send a message to adults that young people are ready to contribute to shaping their own lives and schools. The people in the video tell their stories, but you do not need to tell your story. You can think about the questions using the youth club example, or a group you know.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Never ask learners to talk about their own home, family, past or times they did not belong. The youth club, a class, a team, a group of friends, a language or a hobby always work as examples.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: Never ask learners to tell about home, family, the past or times they were not allowed to belong anywhere. The youth club, a classroom, a team, a group of friends, a language or an interest can always be used as examples.

sensitiveNotes.2.source: If a learner chooses to share something personal, listen calmly, thank them, and do not ask follow-up questions in front of the group. Follow your centre's safeguarding steps if you are worried.
sensitiveNotes.2.back: If a learner chooses by themselves to share something personal, listen calmly, thank them and do not ask more in front of the group. Follow the centre's child protection steps if you are worried.
